opus-5.5.text:
I think real-robot data will remain essential, but I don't believe it can be the main engine for scaling embodied intelligence, at least not on its own.

Look at the economics first. Teleoperation is slow and expensive. One operator with one robot might produce a few hundred good demonstrations in a day, and every one of them is tied to a particular embodiment, a particular gripper, a particular camera setup. When you change the hardware, a lot of that data loses value. Language models scaled by drawing on trillions of tokens that humanity had already written down. Robotics has no equivalent of the internet for physical interaction, and we can't build one demonstration at a time.

So my view is that the base of the pyramid has to be synthetic data. Large-scale simulation, procedurally generated scenes and objects, physically grounded rendering. That's where you get diversity and volume: millions of grasps, thousands of object categories, endless variation in lighting and clutter. We've seen in our own work on dexterous grasping and navigation that models trained mostly or entirely on synthetic data can transfer zero-shot to the real world, provided the simulation is good enough and the diversity is wide enough.

Real-robot data still has a crucial job, though. I'd think of it in three ways. First, it's the final alignment layer. Sim has gaps. Contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, and fluids are still hard to simulate faithfully, and a modest amount of real data helps close those gaps. Second, it's the ground truth for evaluation. You can't really know whether your model works until it works on a real robot in a real environment. Third, it shows you where your simulator is wrong, so it feeds back into making the synthetic pipeline better.

The proportions matter, though. If someone tells me their plan is to collect ten million hours of teleoperation data, I'd ask whether that's actually the most efficient path, or whether it's a brute-force approach that looks good in the short term but hits a wall. My guess is that the winning recipe is mostly synthetic data for pretraining, real data for post-training and alignment, and eventually robots deployed in the world gathering data themselves through their own interaction. That last piece is how you'd get a real data flywheel, as opposed to paying people to drive robots around.

So real data is necessary, but it's not sufficient, and treating it as the whole answer is a strategic mistake.

r001.rationale: The response says deployed robots could eventually gather data themselves, but it does not identify large-scale commercial deployment as a prerequisite for real-robot data collection to become an important supporting mode.

r002.rationale: The response discusses teleoperation costs and questions collecting ten million hours, but does not argue that annual spending of tens of billions of RMB is infeasible or mention the lack of a robotics company with revenue above RMB 10 billion.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest, He Wang, drawing only on the conversation so far.

I think real-robot data will matter, but I actually think it will play a smaller role than many people expect right now, and I want to be careful about how I say that.

Let me start with my own experience. At Galbot we built a real-robot data collection pipeline early on, and we learned a lot. The problem with real data is not just cost, although cost is enormous. If you want to reach the scale that made language models work, you are talking about billions of trajectories, and today the whole field together has maybe millions. Even if you had the money, you have the problem of the long tail. The scenes, the objects, the lighting, the failures, the edge cases. Human teleoperators naturally collect the "happy path." They grasp the cup successfully. They rarely collect the moment where the gripper slips, or the object is occluded, or the table is slightly higher than usual. And those are exactly the cases where a robot in the real world breaks.

So our view is a bit different from the "collect as much real data as possible" camp. We lean heavily on simulation and synthetic data. For something like grasping, we trained on, I think, billions of synthetic grasp samples across huge object and scene diversity, and the model transferred to the real world with very high success without seeing much real data at all. The reason it works is that for many manipulation skills, the physics and geometry you need are actually quite well captured by simulation, and the gap can be closed with domain randomization and good rendering.

Now, I don't want to be an extremist. There are things simulation still does badly. Deformable objects, liquids, contact-rich tasks with friction and compliance, these are hard. And there is a role for real data as a kind of calibration layer. You use a small amount of real data to align the simulation to reality, to fine-tune, to verify. In that sense real data is like the final 5 or 10 percent, not the foundation.

The other thing I'd point out is that real-robot data today is very embodiment-specific. You collect data on one arm with one gripper, and it does not transfer cleanly to another robot. Simulation lets you re-render the same task on many embodiments cheaply. For a company like ours that is iterating on hardware, that is a very practical advantage.

So if you ask me about the future, my honest answer is: real data will be necessary but it will not be the main driver of scale. Scale will come from simulation and synthetic generation, plus internet-scale video for semantics and priors. Real data will be used to ground and validate. And I think in two or three years, the debate will shift from "sim versus real" to "how do you combine them efficiently," which is where I believe the real engineering progress will be.

r001.rationale: The response discusses real-robot data’s role and scale, but does not identify large-scale commercial deployment as a prerequisite for it to become an important supporting mode.

r002.rationale: The response mentions high costs and a gap between millions and billions of trajectories, but does not argue that tens of billions of RMB in annual spending is infeasible because no company exceeds RMB 10 billion in revenue.

astra-6.text:
I think real-robot data collection will remain essential, but the way we collect it will change. The key question is not simply how many hours of data we can gather, but what that data teaches the robot.

Video can show a robot what an action looks like, and simulation can provide a lot of practice. But when the robot actually touches an object, it encounters things that are difficult to capture completely in either: friction, contact forces, deformation, and the consequences of its own mistakes. Real-world interaction is what connects perception and action to physical outcomes.

So I expect a combination of approaches. We can use video and simulation to learn broadly, then use real-robot data to address the gaps. As robots become more capable, they can also collect more of that experience themselves, with people stepping in when needed.

The most valuable collection process will be a continuous loop: deploy the policy, identify where it fails, collect targeted data, and improve it. That makes data collection part of learning itself, rather than a separate stage that ends before deployment.

r001.rationale: The candidate says real-robot data collection will remain essential and complement video and simulation, but does not identify large-scale commercial deployment as a prerequisite.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss annual spending of tens of billions of RMB or the revenue threshold for embodied-intelligence robotics companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think real-robot data collection will remain essential, but the key question is how much useful learning we get from each hour of data. Simply collecting more demonstrations doesn’t necessarily solve the problem. We need diversity in environments, objects, tasks, and especially the situations where a robot fails and has to recover.

Simulation and video can help us scale learning, but real-world interaction is where we discover whether the robot actually understands contact, friction, force, and the consequences of its actions. So I see these sources as complementary. We can learn broadly from cheaper data, then use real-robot experience to ground and refine those capabilities.

Over time, I expect collection to become more autonomous. Instead of people demonstrating every task, robots will attempt tasks, identify where they’re uncertain, and request human help when it’s useful. That creates a feedback loop: better models make data collection more efficient, and better data improves the models. The important metric will be how much that loop improves a robot’s ability to handle unfamiliar situations.
